venue_date: arXiv preprint, submitted 2 February 2026; cs.AI (primary), cs.LG. No journal_ref or venue comment — appears to be an unrefereed preprint as of 2026-09.
what_it_does: Proposes Causal Prompt Optimization (CPO), which reframes automatic prompt optimization as causal estimation. Stage 1 learns an OFFLINE causal reward model by applying Double Machine Learning to semantic embeddings of prompts and queries, so the causal effect of prompt variation is isolated from confounding query attributes (their stated failure mode of existing offline reward models is that they are "fundamentally correlational"). Stage 2 uses that debiased reward signal to drive a resource-efficient search for query-specific prompts without online LLM evaluation. Evaluated on math reasoning, visualization, and data-analytics benchmarks; reported gains come mainly from robustness on hard queries, and the cost argument is that per-query customization moves from real-time inference to an offline causal model.
summary_accurate: yes — the claim is essentially verbatim from the abstract. Authors confirmed as Wei Chen, Yanbin Fang, Shuran Fu, Fasheng Xu, Xuan Wei, so "Chen et al." is correct. Two cautions worth carrying into a write-up: (a) it is a preprint with no peer review, and (b) the DML is applied to embeddings as the nuisance-adjustment features, i.e. it is a reward-model debiasing device, not a formal identification result — there is no identification theorem for the prompt-as-treatment estimand, and the treatment is a continuous embedding with no stated overlap/positivity argument. Calling it "causal identification of prompt effects" would be overstated; calling it "DML-debiased offline reward model for prompt selection" is right.
relevance_to_us: Closest prior work to a single-round version of our setup: prompt = treatment, query = covariate, reward = outcome, embeddings = the nuisance-adjustment representation. It is the natural T=1 baseline/comparison for a multi-round DTR formulation, and it also concedes the key weakness we can push on: it is static/one-shot, has no notion of sequential prompts, no time-varying confounding from earlier turns, and no policy-value guarantee — just a debiased reward plus greedy search.

Describing it as "the first paper to frame instructions as a treatment" is fair; describing it as "rigorous causal identification of instruction effects" would be overstated.

true_title: Causal Effect Estimation with Latent Textual Treatments
venue_date: arXiv preprint, submitted 17 February 2026; cs.CL (primary), econ.EM. No journal_ref or venue comment — unrefereed preprint as of 2026-09. Authors: Omri Feldman, Amar Venugopal, Jann Spiess, Amir Feder.

Their central statistical point is that naive estimation is significantly biased because text "inherently conflates treatment and covariate information": the same text carries both the intervened feature and the nuisance/covariate content, so adjusting on the text representation adjusts on the treatment too. The bias mechanism ("text mixes treatment and nuisance information") and the remedy (residualization) are both accurate to the abstract. Two refinements: (a) it is COVARIATE residualization — the covariate/text representation is residualized with respect to the treatment, not the treatment residualized with respect to text — so "they propose residualization" is right but which object gets residualized matters if we build on the estimator; (b) the setting is a controlled/randomized text experiment with SAE-steered latent treatments, not observational text, so the bias is an adjustment-set/overcontrol problem rather than classical confounding. Saying "conditioning on text embeddings induces bias" is accurate; implying the paper is about observational confounding would be overstated.
relevance_to_us: This is the strongest theoretical warning for our design and the most directly usable result of the three: if we adjust on an embedding of the prompt or of the conversation history, that embedding contains the treatment, and we induce exactly the bias they characterize. Their residualization fix transfers to our nuisance construction, and the Spiess/Feder econ.EM framing is the right register for our own bias argument. Note the tension with item 1, which does DML on prompt AND query embeddings jointly — by this paper's argument that is precisely the conflation that needs residualizing, which is a citable critique of CPO.

Three requirements it imposes: (1) never let the loop use ground-truth to decide when to stop -- your termination rule must be answerable at inference time, or the result is invalid; (2) report a SELF-CONSISTENCY baseline at MATCHED total token/call budget, because that is the bar multi-round methods keep failing, not greedy single-pass CoT; (3) if your rounds help, you must be able to name the external signal supplying the information, since this paper's mechanism claim is that an unaided model cannot tell a right answer from a wrong one and so revision is a random walk downhill. Note the scoping that leaves room for you: the title says 'Yet', and the claim is specifically about INTRINSIC correction on reasoning -- verifier-in-the-loop, trained self-correction, and non-reasoning objectives are all outside its scope.

venue_date: arXiv preprint, submitted 2026-06-25. Authors: Martha Barnard, Jared D. Huling, Julian Wolfson. No journal reference yet.
what_it_does: Studies causal effects of function-valued (hence infinite-dimensional) treatments, motivated by accelerometer-measured physical activity over continuous time. It proposes *stochastic policies* for functional treatments that identify the effect of changing the treatment distribution WITHOUT requiring a positivity assumption, and handles temporal confounding over continuous time. The construction modifies the treatment through a single analyst-chosen basis function, which gives explicit control over the modification and over temporal confounding feedback. Establishes asymptotic normality and rate double robustness of the estimators; applied to NHANES to estimate the effect of increasing physical activity over three-hour periods on mortality. The paper's own framing contrasts this with modified functional treatment policies (MFTPs), which use a deterministic rule on the natural value of treatment.
summary_accurate: This is the closest real precedent to the "infinite-dimensional action space" half of item (4), and it is 2026 and genuine (arXiv API returns exactly this title, authors and date). It is NOT text: the action space is a space of real-valued functions, and the whole technique -- modification via one basis function -- depends on that linear structure, which text does not have. So cite it as proof of concept that positivity-free stochastic policies extend to infinite-dimensional treatments, not as coverage of text.
relevance_to_us: Strongest available support for the claim that the positivity-free stochastic-policy idea is not intrinsically limited to scalar treatments. Also a useful template for the move you likely need: pick a low-dimensional, analyst-controlled direction in which to perturb a high-dimensional natural action, and define the estimand along that direction.

claimed: (4-candidate) Natural language as the action space in a dynamic treatment regime framework
true_title: Policy Learning with a Natural Language Action Space: A Causal Approach
venue_date: arXiv preprint (cs.CL), submitted 2025-02-24. Authors: Bohan Zhang, Yixin Wang, Paramveer S. Dhillon. No journal reference.
what_it_does: Proposes a causal framework for multi-stage decision-making in natural language action spaces where the outcome is observed only after a sequence of actions. Uses Q-learning to estimate Dynamic Treatment Regimes through a single model, learning policies by gradient ascent on language embeddings, with a decoding strategy that maps optimized embeddings back to coherent natural language. Evaluated on mental health intervention, hate speech countering and sentiment transfer, against PPO-style baselines, with human evaluation of transfer strength, content preservation and fluency.
summary_accurate: Real paper, correctly described by its title -- but it is NOT what item (4) asks for. It is *optimal-policy learning* (Q-learning for an optimal DTR) in a language action space, not stochastic interventions or modified treatment policies, and the abstract and framing are method/empirical rather than identification-theoretic; the arXiv page states no explicit identification assumptions, and there is no positivity analysis. Anyone who summarized this as "MTPs with a text action space" would be overstating it substantially.
relevance_to_us: Directly adjacent prior work for a multi-round LLM DTR project -- you must cite and distinguish it, because a reviewer will ask. Your differentiator is precisely what it lacks: an identification argument, and a stochastic/modified-policy estimand that does not require positivity over a text action space.

claimed: (4-candidate) Text-as-treatment causal inference with formal identification and overlap handling
true_title: Causal Inference with Generative Artificial Intelligence: Application to Texts as Treatments
venue_date: arXiv preprint, v1 2024-10-01, latest revision 2026-06-11. Authors: Kosuke Imai, Kentaro Nakamura. No journal reference yet (note: an earlier version circulated under the title "Causal Representation Learning with Generative Artificial Intelligence...").
what_it_does: Uses a deep generative model (an LLM) to *generate* the treatment texts and then uses the LLM's own true internal representation of the generated text for effect estimation, so that treatment features of interest (a sentiment, a topic) are disentangled from unknown confounding features without having to learn a causal representation from data. This GenAI-Powered Inference (GPI) approach formally establishes conditions for nonparametric identification of the ATE, proposes an estimation strategy explicitly designed to AVOID VIOLATION OF THE OVERLAP ASSUMPTION, and derives asymptotic properties via double machine learning; extended with an instrumental-variables argument when the treatment feature is based on human perception, and applicable to text reuse where an LLM regenerates existing texts.
summary_accurate: Genuine and highly relevant, with one boundary to respect: it is a POINT-TREATMENT (single-stage) framework. There is no time-varying confounding, no sequential randomization, no g-formula, and no modified treatment policy. Its overlap argument comes from controlling the text-generating process, not from redefining the estimand as a natural-value-dependent policy. So it does not answer the longitudinal question you care about.
relevance_to_us: The most rigorous existing treatment of text as a treatment, and the natural thing your longitudinal proposal generalizes. Its overlap strategy -- generate the treatment yourself so you know the true representation and the propensity structure -- is a real alternative to the LMTP support-condition route, and you should say why you are not simply doing that in the multi-round setting.

claimed: tau-bench user simulation (named in task as a multi-turn benchmark where the user side is generated)
true_title: $\tau$-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
venue_date: arXiv 17 Jun 2024; Sierra AI (Yao, Shinn, Razavi, Narasimhan); widely cited, later at ICLR 2025
what_it_does: Builds two domains (115 retail + 50 airline tasks) with realistic databases, API tools and a written domain policy; the agent must resolve a request through multi-turn dialogue with an LLM-simulated user (originally gpt-4-0613). Headline result: GPT-4o under 50% success, pass^8 < 25% in retail.
summary_accurate: yes — the user side is LLM-generated, not scripted. One nuance often overstated elsewhere: the user simulator is prompt-based and uncalibrated against real humans; the paper itself does no human-vs-simulator validation.
relevance_to_us: This is the canonical 'simulated user as environment' setup that later sim2real work attacks. pass^k is a useful variance-aware metric for DTR-style policy comparison, but the environment is a prompt-driven user, so any policy learned/evaluated in it inherits simulator bias.

claimed: tau2-bench user simulation (named in task)
true_title: $\tau^2$-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
venue_date: arXiv 9 Jun 2025 (Sierra AI; Barres et al.)
what_it_does: Extends tau-bench to a dual-control Dec-POMDP: the simulated user also has tools and can change shared environment state (Telecom domain), so the agent must coordinate and instruct, not just answer. Adds a compositional task generator producing verifiable tasks from atomic components, and a user simulator whose behavior is constrained by tools and observable state rather than free-form roleplay. Ablations separate reasoning failures from communication/coordination failures; performance drops sharply moving from no-user to dual-control.
summary_accurate: yes. The important detail for us is that the simulator is deliberately *constrained by environment state* — this is the main existing answer to 'how do you stop a prompt-based user from hallucinating'.
relevance_to_us: Tool/state-grounding the user is a cheap way to bound simulator error without learning a user policy. Directly transferable trick if we need a simulator as a behavior model.

claimed: MT-Bench-101 (named in task as a multi-turn benchmark with scripted vs generated user side)
true_title: MT-Bench-101: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Multi-Turn Dialogues
venue_date: ACL 2024 Main (Long); arXiv 22 Feb 2024, v3 5 Nov 2024 (Bai, Liu, Bu et al.)
what_it_does: A three-tier ability taxonomy (perceptivity, adaptability, interactivity) over 13 tasks, instantiated as 1,388 multi-turn dialogues / 4,208 turns across 30 topics. Dialogues were GPT-4-generated then human-curated by five annotators, so the user turns are FIXED SCRIPTS replayed to every model under test — there is no live simulator. Evaluated 21 LLMs with a GPT-4 judge reporting ~87% agreement with human experts.
summary_accurate: yes, and the scripted/generated distinction matters: MT-Bench-101 is the scripted end of the spectrum. Claims that it 'simulates users' would be overstated — it is a static replay benchmark.
relevance_to_us: Scripted replay removes simulator stochasticity but also removes counterfactual user reaction, so it cannot evaluate a *policy* that changes the conversation trajectory. This is exactly the limitation a DTR formulation has to escape.

claimed: MultiChallenge (named in task)
true_title: MultiChallenge: A Realistic Multi-Turn Conversation Evaluation Benchmark Challenging to Frontier LLMs
venue_date: Findings of ACL 2025; arXiv 29 Jan 2025 (Sirdeshmukh, Deshpande, Mols et al., Scale AI)
what_it_does: Targets four failure modes observed in real human-LLM chats: instruction retention, inference memory of user information, reliable versioned editing, and self-coherence. Human-written multi-turn contexts are replayed (scripted user side) and the final model turn is graded by an LLM judge with instance-level rubrics. Frontier models score under 50%; Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Jun 2024) at 41.4% average at publication.
summary_accurate: yes. Note it is a scripted-context benchmark with a judged final turn, not a user simulator; also there is now an 'Audio MultiChallenge' follow-up (arXiv:2512.14865) I did not verify in depth.
relevance_to_us: Good source of *failure taxonomies* grounded in real logs, which is what a learned user policy has to reproduce. Its rubric-per-instance judging is a template for turn-level outcome labels.

claimed: CollabLLM (named in task; uses a simulated user to improve an assistant)
true_title: CollabLLM: From Passive Responders to Active Collaborators
venue_date: ICML 2025, Outstanding Paper Award; arXiv 2 Feb 2025, v3 29 Jul 2025 (Shirley Wu, Galley, Peng, Cheng, ... Leskovec, Gao — Stanford/Microsoft)
what_it_does: Trains an assistant with Multiturn-aware Rewards (MR): from each candidate response it rolls forward simulated continuations, sampling both assistant and simulated-user turns with added stochasticity, and credits the response by the long-term value of those rollouts. Critically, it closes the loop with a 201-judge human study showing +17.6% satisfaction and -10.4% user time.
summary_accurate: accurate, and it is one of the few in this whole area that validates against real humans. Two caveats often dropped: the simulator is prompt-based (not learned from logs), and the forward rollouts are a *training-time* credit-assignment device, not inference-time search.
relevance_to_us: This is the closest published analogue to a model-based DTR: simulated rollouts give a multi-turn value estimate used for credit assignment on a single action. Our angle differentiates if we learn the user model from logs and/or do the rollout at decision time.

claimed: WildChat as a public dataset of real human-LLM multi-turn conversations

It is the most linguistically and toxicity-diverse public corpus of organic prompts.
summary_accurate: summary accurate, but the license claim in the paper is STALE: the paper says AI2 ImpACT; the live HF card for allenai/WildChat-1M is ODC-BY and ungated. No turn-level outcome or quality labels — only moderation/toxicity scores and boolean flags.
relevance_to_us: Best-scale observational log for fitting a user policy (utterance-level behavior conditioned on history + coarse demographics). No reward labels, so outcomes must be derived (see WildFeedback) — and there is no treatment randomization, so confounding by user intent is severe.

venue_date: ICLR 2024; arXiv 21 Sep 2023 (Zheng, Chiang, Sheng et al., LMSYS)

summary_accurate: accurate. Licensing is the practical catch: it is GATED under a bespoke 'LMSYS-Chat-1M Dataset License Agreement' (non-transferable, no redistribution, creators may demand deletion, must also honor each model's own terms). No turn-level outcome labels — only language tags, OpenAI moderation output, and a redaction flag.
relevance_to_us: Usable as logs but the ~2-turn mean and the no-redistribution clause both hurt; shallow trajectories limit horizon for DTR. Its sibling (Chatbot Arena Conversations) is where the human preference labels live.

claimed: PRISM as a public dataset of real human-LLM multi-turn conversations

venue_date: arXiv 23 Jan 2026 (v2 28 Jan 2026); ACL 2026 Long. (Also appears on the ICLR 2026 virtual site, so the venue listing is slightly inconsistent across sources.) Seshadri, Cahyawijaya, Odumakinde, Singh, Goldfarb-Tarrant (UC Irvine / Cohere)

claimed: (search hypothesis) learns a user policy from logs / grounded simulation
true_title: RealUserSim: Bridging the Reality Gap in Agent Benchmarking via Grounded User Simulation
venue_date: arXiv (abs page reads 'Submitted on 7 Apr 2026', which is inconsistent with the 2605 = May-2026 identifier — minor metadata anomaly, paper itself resolves correctly). Ming Zhu, Juntao Tan, Rithesh Murthy, ... Savarese, Heinecke, Huan Wang (Salesforce). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

relevance_to_us: A log-derived *profile* representation (extract executable behavior programs from logs, then condition) is a middle path between prompting and full policy learning — cheaper than fine-tuning and auditable. The 6-8% style-match number is a good quantitative hook for our motivation.

claimed: (search hypothesis) decision-level rather than style-level simulator fidelity
true_title: Simulated Customers Never Walk Away: Decision Fidelity of LLM User Simulators Measured Against Real Purchase Outcomes
venue_date: arXiv 16 Jun 2026 (Liang Chen); cs.AI/cs.CL/cs.HC, no venue listed
what_it_does: Argues existing simulator evaluation only checks whether simulators *talk* like humans, never whether they *decide* like humans, and introduces 'decision fidelity' measured against 2,790 production conversations with real customers including 793 with verified payment records. Finds a systematic 'disengagement deficit': simulators reproduce eventual purchasers well but badly misrepresent non-buyers, showing half the resistance and twice the deliberation of real non-buyers, who simply disengage. The bias holds across model families and is not fixed by explicitly instructing the simulator that it may walk away.
summary_accurate: accurate. Single-author preprint with proprietary data, so treat the exact numbers as not independently reproducible — but the mechanism (no abandonment) is corroborated by the cooperativeness findings in 2603.11245 and 2605.12894.
relevance_to_us: This is the most damaging finding for our purposes: simulators cannot represent the ABSORBING STATE (user quits). A DTR whose reward depends on continuation/dropout will be systematically misestimated if trained or evaluated in simulation. Worth citing as the specific bias we must handle.

claimed: (search hypothesis) framework for measuring simulated-vs-real user differences
true_title: Synthetic Users, Real Differences: an Evaluation Framework for User Simulation in Multi-Turn Conversations
venue_date: arXiv 4 May 2026 (Yu Lu Liu, Hyokun Yun, Tanya Roosta, Ziang Xiao); cs.CL, no venue listed
what_it_does: Proposes 'realsim', an 8-dimension framework (communication functions, user states, message characteristics) for comparing synthetic to real human-chatbot dialogue, evaluated on 1,000 real multi-turn conversations spanning 16 chatbot application domains. Core finding is that synthetic users fail to reproduce the communication FRICTIONS real users introduce, making simulation-based evaluation systematically optimistic. Also finds the gap varies by domain, arguing for domain-specific rather than general-purpose simulators.
summary_accurate: accurate but it is a descriptive/diagnostic framework — it measures the gap, it does not close it and it does not test downstream transfer.
relevance_to_us: Useful as an off-the-shelf fidelity instrument for auditing whatever user model we build. The domain-specificity finding argues against borrowing someone else's simulator.

claimed: (search hypothesis) behavioral comparison of human vs agent users
true_title: Human vs. Agent in Task-Oriented Conversations
venue_date: SIGIR-AP 2025; arXiv 22 Sep 2025 (v2 5 Nov 2025). Zhefan Wang, Ning Geng, Zhiqiang Guo, Weizhi Ma, Min Zhang (Tsinghua)
what_it_does: Defines a ten-dimension comparison framework across three categories — conversation strategy, interaction style, conversation evaluation — and applies it to matched human-user and LLM-user conversations in four task-oriented scenarios. Positions itself as diagnostic guidance for building better simulators.

claimed: (search hypothesis) dataset + validation framework with real human-AI conversations and counterfactual agent quality
true_title: ConvApparel: A Benchmark Dataset and Validation Framework for User Simulators in Conversational Recommenders
venue_date: EACL 2026 Long (Rabat); Meshi, Balog, Goldman, Caciularu, Tennenholtz, Jeong, Globerson, Boutilier (Google Research/DeepMind). Google Research blog post 9 Apr 2026. Dataset released on Hugging Face
what_it_does: Releases 4,000+ human-AI apparel-shopping conversations (~15,000 turns) collected with a DUAL-AGENT randomized protocol: participants were routed, blind, to either a deliberately helpful 'Good' recommender or a deliberately unhelpful 'Bad' one, and annotated their own satisfaction and frustration turn by turn. Proposes a three-part validation framework: population-level statistical alignment, an automated human-likeness discriminator score, and counterfactual validation (does a simulator fit on Good-agent data react realistically to Bad-agent behavior it never saw?). Finds a significant realism gap across all simulators — synthetic dialogue stays detectable — but data-driven simulators (ICL and SFT) beat prompt-only baselines and the best ones generalize out-of-distribution to frustrating agent behavior.
summary_accurate: accurate. Caution: the Google Research blog post is titled 'ConvApparel: Measuring and bridging the realism gap in user simulators' and lists only Meshi and Goldman — cite the arXiv/anthology title and full author list, not the blog.
relevance_to_us: The single most important find for this project. Randomized Good/Bad agent assignment plus first-person turn-level satisfaction labels is effectively a randomized multi-stage trial in conversation form — so we get identification without relying on unconfoundedness, and we get a real counterfactual-validation criterion for a user model. Small domain (apparel shopping) but the design is what we want to imitate.

claimed: (search hypothesis) purpose-built user language models trained from real conversations
true_title: Flipping the Dialogue: Training and Evaluating User Language Models
venue_date: Accepted at ICLR 2026; arXiv 8 Oct 2025, v2 22 Mar 2026. Tarek Naous, Philippe Laban, Wei Xu, Jennifer Neville (Georgia Tech / Microsoft Research)
what_it_does: Argues assistant LMs are structurally bad user simulators because they are post-trained toward polished, cooperative, complete responses, and instead post-trains dedicated 'User LMs' to follow a defined user intent and produce natural, iterative, partially-specified human-like turns. Shows User LMs align better with real human behavior and are more robust simulators than prompted assistants. Downstream effect is large: GPT-4o's success on coding and math tasks falls from 74.6% to 57.4% when the user side is a realistic User LM instead of a cooperative prompted simulator.
summary_accurate: accurate — this is the strongest 'learn a user policy' result and the 74.6 -> 57.4 drop is the cleanest evidence that simulator fidelity changes conclusions, not just cosmetics.
relevance_to_us: This is our closest methodological neighbor for the behavior-model half of a DTR: a learned generative user policy conditioned on latent intent. Same group as LLMs-Get-Lost (2505.06120), and the intent-conditioning is essentially a latent-state assumption we may want to make explicit.

claimed: (search hypothesis) RL-trained user simulators
true_title: Learning User Simulators with Turing Rewards
venue_date: arXiv 17 Jun 2026, v2 25 Jun 2026. Yingshan Susan Wang, Cedegao E. Zhang, Linlu Qiu, Zexue He, Pengyuan Li, Alex Pentland, Roger P. Levy, Yoon Kim (MIT); cs.CL, no venue listed
what_it_does: Replaces token-matching objectives with Turing-RL: an LLM judge acts as a discriminator scoring how indistinguishable a generated user turn is from the real user's actual turn, and that discriminative score is the RL reward. Evaluated on conversational chat and Reddit discussion data. Concludes that optimizing for indistinguishability beats optimizing for response matching when learning user simulators.
summary_accurate: accurate. It is an adversarial/GAN-flavored objective — note the usual caveat that indistinguishability under a fixed judge does not guarantee correct conditional distributions or correct decision behavior (cf. the disengagement deficit in 2606.20708).
relevance_to_us: Relevant if we fit a user model by likelihood and find it too smooth/cooperative. But for DTR we care about calibrated conditional outcome distributions, not fooling a discriminator, so this objective may be the wrong one for us — worth citing as a contrast.

claimed: (search hypothesis) measures simulator quality by downstream effect on real humans
true_title: Quantifying the Utility of User Simulators for Building Collaborative LLM Assistants
venue_date: arXiv 10 May 2026. Joseph Suh, Ayush Raj, Minwoo Kang, Serina Chang (UC Berkeley); cs.CL, no venue listed
what_it_does: Defines simulator quality extrinsically: train assistants by RL against different simulators, then measure the resulting assistants against REAL humans. In a 283-participant user study, assistants trained against log-grounded fine-tuned simulators win 58% vs 51% for assistants trained against role-playing prompted simulators. Ablations: persona conditioning helps prompted simulators only marginally, model scale helps fine-tuned but not prompted simulators, and assistants trained on prompted simulators generalize worse.
summary_accurate: accurate, and this is the right way to frame the question. Caveat: 58% vs 51% is a real but modest gap, so 'fine-tuned simulators are vastly superior' (as some secondary summaries put it) is OVERSTATED — the win-rate delta is ~7 points.
relevance_to_us: Gives us the evaluation criterion we should adopt: judge a user model by the real-human performance of the policy it produces, i.e. treat it as an instrument for policy value rather than a thing to be scored on its own. Also the cleanest existing evidence that log-grounding actually transfers.

claimed: (search hypothesis) causal treatment of simulator controllability
true_title: Controllable User Simulation
venue_date: arXiv 12 May 2026. Guy Tennenholtz, Ofer Meshi, Amir Globerson, Uri Shalit, Jihwan Jeong, Craig Boutilier (Google Research/DeepMind + Technion); cs.AI/cs.CL/cs.LG
what_it_does: Frames controllable simulation as causal inference and shows that the standard recipe — SFT a simulator on post-hoc trajectory-level labels (e.g. 'this user was frustrated') — induces LOOK-AHEAD BIAS, because the label leaks future information into the conditioning, breaking causal consistency. Under policy shift this produces 'controllability collapse', where the variance of counterfactual evaluation metrics explodes. Proposes three fixes — a priori controls, step-wise dynamic controls, and policy-conditioned learning — and shows they remove look-ahead bias while preserving natural behavioral variance.
summary_accurate: accurate and technically the most rigorous paper in this set.
relevance_to_us: HIGHEST methodological relevance. Look-ahead bias from post-hoc labels is exactly the failure mode we would walk into if we conditioned a user model on trajectory-level outcomes from logs, and 'variance explodes under policy shift' is the standard OPE overlap problem in disguise. Same group as ConvApparel — read these two together.

venue_date: SCI-CHAT workshop (Simulation of Conversational Intelligence in Chat) @ EACL 2024; arXiv 29 Jan 2024. Kaustubh D. Dhole (Emory), single author
what_it_does: Builds two GPT-J-based user simulators — a Retrieval Augmented Simulator and a Summary Controlled Simulator — to generate more diverse interaction data than plain prompting. summary_accurate: accurate for what it is; do not treat it as state of the art. Workshop paper, GPT-J era, no human validation.

Two things to carry over honestly: the formula is derived under working assumptions S1 (bounded responder/non-responder variance gap; responder covariance <= non-responder covariance) and S2 (exchangeable marginal covariance, constant variance across time and regime), and the authors themselves call eq. (10) conservative, sharpest badness near rho ~ 0.62, with a sharper version in their Appendix C.
relevance_to_us: This is the formula you actually need. Verbatim: n >= [4(z_{1-alpha/2} + z_{1-beta})^2 / delta^2] * (1 - rho^2) * DE, where delta = Delta/sigma is the standardized end-of-study effect, rho is the exchangeable within-person correlation, and DE is the design effect from their Table 3: Design I (everyone re-randomized) DE = 2; Design II (only non-responders re-randomized) DE = (1/2)(2 - r_1) + (1/2)(2 - r_{-1}), conservatively 2; Design III (non-responders to one first-stage option only) DE = (1/2)(3 - r_1), conservatively 3/2, with r_{a1} = P(R(a1) = 1) the response rate to first-stage option a1. Set rho = 0 to recover the single-end-of-study-measurement case. Note the 4: it is the price of splitting the sample across two randomizations, not a typo for 2.

An MRT randomizes the same unit at many decision points and gets its power from N x T, not from N alone -- exactly the structure of a conversation with many turns. Your 'A_t as a time-varying treatment, H_t as time-varying covariate' framing IS the MRT framing; say so and cite this.

claimed: MRT sample-size formula: Liao, Klasnja, Tewari, Murphy (2016), Statistics in Medicine
true_title: Sample size calculations for micro-randomized trials in mHealth
venue_date: Statistics in Medicine 35(12):1944-1971, 2016
what_it_does: Gives the test statistic and the sample-size calculator for detecting a time-varying proximal treatment effect in an MRT. Working model for the available decision points (availability indicator I_t = 1): E[Y_{t+1} | I_t = 1, H_t, A_t] = B_t'alpha + (A_t - rho_t) Z_t'beta, with rho_t = P(A_t = 1) the KNOWN randomization probability, B_t a q-dimensional nuisance basis and Z_t a p-dimensional effect basis (e.g. quadratic in t). Fit by UNWEIGHTED least squares -- they show explicitly that a non-identity GEE working correlation makes the estimating equations have nonzero mean and biases beta, because both availability I_t and Y_{t+1} can be affected by past treatment. Robust variance Sigma_beta = Q^{-1} W Q^{-1} with Q = sum_t E[I_t] rho_t (1 - rho_t) Z_t Z_t'.
summary_accurate: accurate, and the paper is more careful than its reputation: the centering of A_t by rho_t and the refusal to use a non-identity working correlation are load-bearing, not stylistic.
relevance_to_us: Here is the formula form you asked for, verbatim in structure. Test H0: beta(t) = 0 for all t with the Wald-type statistic N * betahat' Sigmahat_beta^{-1} betahat, rejecting when it exceeds [(N - q - p) / (p(N - q - 1))] * F^{-1}_{p, N-q-p}(1 - alpha_0) (a Hotelling T-squared / F critical value, with Mancl-DeRouen hat-matrix small-sample adjustment to What). Under H1: beta(t)/sigmabar = d(t), the statistic is approximately noncentral chi-squared with noncentrality c_N = N * d' (sum_{t=1}^{T} E[I_t] rho_t (1 - rho_t) Z_t Z_t') d, where sigmabar^2 = (1/T) sum_t E[Var(Y_{t+1} | I_t = 1, A_t)] is the average residual variance and d = beta/sigmabar the standardized effect vector. N solves F_{p, N-q-p; c_N}(F^{-1}_{p, N-q-p}(1 - alpha_0)) = 1 - beta_0. Inputs: {Z_t}, d, the availability pattern {E[I_t]}, alpha_0, power 1 - beta_0. Working assumptions (a) correct nuisance model, (b) beta(t) = Z_t'beta, (c) Var(Y_{t+1}|I_t=1,A_t) constant in t and A_t, (d) residual autocovariance not depending on A_t, A_s. THE KEY DESIGN FACT FOR US: information enters only through Q = sum_t E[I_t] rho_t (1-rho_t) Z_t Z_t'. So N scales down roughly like 1/(T * rho(1-rho) * availability). Their HeartSteps table shows N = 32-193 for average standardized proximal effects of 0.05-0.10 over T ~ 210 decision points. That is why a many-turn design is cheap and a 2-stage SMART is expensive -- quantify this in the pre-registration. Note rho(1-rho) is maximized at rho = 0.5, which also bounds how many prompt classes you can afford per decision point (your Q7).

what_it_does: Defines the causal excursion effect -- the contrast in proximal outcome between excursion policies that deviate from the trial's randomization policy, marginal over some of the history -- and gives the centered-and-weighted least squares (C-WLS) estimator for it, with semiparametric inference. relevance_to_us: This is your identification-theory anchor and it maps onto your Q1 default almost exactly. Your gamma_t(H_t, a, a_ref) is a causal excursion effect. Cite Boruvka et al. for the estimator and the centering/weighting trick rather than reinventing it -- and note explicitly that centering by the known propensity is what buys robustness to a misspecified model of prior output quality, which is precisely the confounder-affected-by-prior-treatment problem in your COORDINATION.md.

claimed: A published randomized experiment in which the randomized/assigned unit is a PROMPT sent to an LLM (Prompting Science Report series)
true_title: Prompting Science Report 1: Prompt Engineering is Complicated and Contingent; Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting; Report 3: I'll pay you or I'll kill you -- but will you care?
true_id: arXiv:2503.04818 (4 Mar 2025); arXiv:2506.07142 (8 Jun 2025); arXiv:2508.00614 (1 Aug 2025). Also SSRN 5165270 / 5285532 / 5375404. A Report 4 ('Playing Pretend: Expert Personas Don't Improve Factual Accuracy', Basil, Shapiro, Shapiro, Mollick, Mollick, Meincke) exists at SSRN 5879722; I did not verify an arXiv id for it.
venue_date: arXiv / SSRN technical reports from Wharton Generative AI Labs, 2025-2026. NOT peer-reviewed venue publications.
what_it_does: Authors (1-3): Lennart Meincke, Ethan Mollick, Lilach Mollick, Dan Shapiro. I pulled the full methods of Report 3. Design: GPQA Diamond (198 PhD-level MCQs) and 100 randomly sampled MMLU-Pro engineering questions; prompt conditions include Baseline, an email shutdown threat, a physical threat, tip-of-$1000, tip-of-$1-trillion, 'important to my career', etc.; models Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o4-mini; temperature 1.0, zero-shot; EVERY question is asked in EVERY condition 25 separate times (4,950 runs per prompt per model on GPQA, 2,500 on MMLU-Pro). This is a fully crossed within-question factorial with 25 replicates per cell, not random assignment of prompts to units -- the only stochasticity is decoding temperature. That is arguably *stronger* than randomization here (the receiver is stateless, so there is no confounding to break), but if you cite these as 'randomized experiments on prompts' a referee will correct you. Also: these are self-published lab reports, not peer-reviewed, and the p-values are uncorrected across a large comparison grid.
relevance_to_us: Three concrete lessons for the harness. (1) Full crossing beats randomization when the receiver is frozen and stateless -- for single-turn contrasts you should fully cross, and reserve randomization for the multi-turn case where history makes crossing infeasible. (2) 25 replicates per (question x condition) cell at temperature 1.0 is the going rate, and they report the 25-vs-100 correlation is high. (3) Their unit of inference is the QUESTION with a paired permutation test -- that is a defensible answer to your Q6 that avoids arguing about the variance form at all. Consider pre-registering a paired randomization/permutation test at the task-instance level as your primary inference, with the cluster-robust sandwich as secondary.

venue_date: arXiv preprint, 20 May 2026
what_it_does: Authors: Victoria Lin, Taedong Yun, Maja Matarić, John Canny, Arthur Gretton, Alexander D'Amour. If the intervener is an LLM conditioned on the history, then changing the assigned prompt class also changes the implicit 'user' the intervener is simulating, and your randomization does not buy what you think it buys. Two mitigations follow from their result and from your own design: (a) prefer the SCRIPTED/templated intervener over a free-form LLM intervener for the anchor design, because a template has no latent persona to drift; (b) adopt their negative-control-outcome diagnostic -- pre-specify invariants of the task instance that must not differ across arms, and report them as a randomization check.
